bode-plot.L1: States that a pole bends the magnitude down by 20 dB per decade and that the corner of an RC circuit is at 1/(RC), with notes open.
bode-plot.L2: Writes H(jω) for an RC or RL filter, computes the corner, and draws the straight-line magnitude and the three-segment phase of a function with real poles and zeros by following the rules.
bode-plot.L3: Explains −3 dB and −45° at a corner from 1 + j; predicts how the curve slides when R or C changes; adds the lines of two or three factors without being told the slopes; says a pole's phase is −5.7° a decade below its corner and why the sketch spreads the turn over two decades.
bode-plot.L4: Reads poles and zeros off a measured Bode plot; knows the sketch is off by 3 dB per factor at a corner and 6 dB where two coincide, that the phase sketch fails when corners are less than a decade apart, and that complex poles need a peak the straight lines cannot show.
missteps: takes the −3 dB point as half the amplitude
puts −90° of phase at the corner
reads 1/(RC) as a frequency in Hz
starts the phase turn at the corner instead of a decade before it
adds a pole's slope only from where the previous one ends, instead of from its own corner

seeds.predict: A low-pass RC with its corner at some ω_c; the capacitor is doubled. Where does the corner go, and what is |H| in dB at the old corner?
seeds.explain: Why the phase of one pole is −45° at its corner and needs two decades to turn by 90°.
seeds.limit: Two poles brought closer together until they coincide: when does the straight-line sketch stop being good to 1 dB?
seeds.transfer: An amplifier with a zero at the origin from a coupling capacitor and a high pole from a load capacitor: sketch its midband and say where its bandwidth ends.

transfer-function.L1: States that H(s) is the ratio of the output's transform to the input's, with the system at rest.
transfer-function.L2: Writes H(s) of an RC, RL or op-amp circuit from impedances, or of a differential equation by replacing d/dt with s.
transfer-function.L3: Reads off H(s) what a circuit does at DC and at very high frequency by letting s go to 0 and to infinity, and says which factor of H(s) each element puts there.
transfer-function.L4: Chooses the form K·Π(1 + s/z)/Π(1 + s/p) to make corners visible, and knows H(s) says nothing about a circuit that was not at rest or that is not linear.
missteps: writes the impedance of a capacitor as jωC instead of 1/(jωC)
forgets the zero at the origin of a high-pass
leaves H(s) in a form whose corners cannot be read off

seeds.predict: A divider of a resistor and a capacitor: which element on top makes it pass low frequencies, and what does H(s) do as s grows?
seeds.explain: Why replacing d/dt by s turns a differential equation into a ratio of polynomials.
seeds.limit: Let s go to 0 and to infinity in H(s) of a filter, and say what each limit means for the circuit.
seeds.transfer: A two-stage circuit with a buffer between the stages: write the overall H(s) and say why the buffer lets the factors multiply.

poles-and-zeros.L1: States that a pole is a value of s where H blows up and a zero one where H vanishes.
poles-and-zeros.L2: Finds the poles and zeros of a rational H(s) and places them in the s-plane.
poles-and-zeros.L3: Explains a pole's effect at s = jω as the vector from the pole to jω: its length sets the magnitude and its angle the phase, so the angle is 45° when ω equals the pole's distance from the origin.
poles-and-zeros.L4: Predicts the response from the pole-zero picture alone, including what a right-half-plane zero does to the phase, and knows when a far pole can be dropped.
missteps: puts the pole of 1/(1 + s/p) at +p instead of −p
treats a zero as removing a frequency completely when it is off the jω axis
measures the angle from the jω axis instead of the σ axis

seeds.predict: A pole at −1000 rad/s: what angle does its vector to j1000 make, and what is its share of |H| there?
seeds.explain: Why a zero on the jω axis blocks a sinusoid completely, and one in the left half-plane only bends the Bode plot.
seeds.limit: A second pole moved further and further from the first: when does it stop mattering at the first pole's corner?
seeds.transfer: A measured phase that keeps falling where the magnitude has flattened: which pole-zero pattern does that point to?

feedback.L1: States the closed-loop gain G/(1 + GH) and that a large loop gain makes it close to 1/H.
feedback.L2: Computes the closed-loop gain of a loop from G and H, and the gain of an op-amp circuit from A and β.
feedback.L3: Explains why the closed-loop gain stops depending on G when GH is large, predicts how much the gain moves when G halves, and identifies the fed-back fraction β in a circuit.
feedback.L4: Knows the benefits (gain set by H, errors and drift divided by 1 + GH) last only where |GH| is large, that the loop must stay negative, and that a loop with too much phase lag can turn positive and oscillate.
missteps: writes G/(1 − GH) for negative feedback
assumes the closed-loop gain halves when G halves
takes H as the gain of the feedback network from input to output instead of output back to input

seeds.predict: A loop with G = 10⁴ and H = 0.01; G drops by a factor of two. By how much does the closed-loop gain change?
seeds.explain: Why feeding back a fraction of the output makes the gain depend on the resistors and not on the amplifier.
seeds.limit: Let GH shrink toward 1 and then below it: what is left of the benefits of feedback?
seeds.transfer: A thermostat that heats in proportion to the temperature error: name G, H and the loop gain, and say what a larger heater does to the steady-state error.

first-order-system.L1: States that one energy store gives one time constant, τ = RC or L/R, and that the step response is an exponential.
first-order-system.L2: Computes τ for a single resistor and writes x(t) = x_final + (x_start − x_final)·e^(−t/τ) for a given start and final value.
first-order-system.L3: Finds the start from the continuity of v_C or i_L, the final value from the t → ∞ circuit and τ from the Thévenin resistance the store sees; says the change is 63% done after τ and 99% after 5τ; connects τ to the corner 1/τ of the frequency response.
first-order-system.L4: Handles a switch that moves again before the transient settles; reads τ off a measured curve; knows the model needs a constant input after the switch and ideal parts, and what an inductor does when its current path is broken.
missteps: uses the nearest resistor instead of the Thévenin resistance for τ
lets v_C or i_L jump at the switching moment
takes the final value of a capacitor with a resistor across it as V_S instead of the divider's value
writes the exponential with the start and final values swapped
thinks the inductor's τ grows with resistance

seeds.predict: A capacitor charged through R₁ with R₂ across it; R₂ is removed. What happens to τ and to the final voltage?
seeds.explain: Why a capacitor's voltage cannot jump but its current can.
seeds.limit: The half period of a square wave made much shorter than τ: what does the capacitor's voltage look like?
seeds.transfer: A sensor with a known time constant read by a sampling circuit: how long after a step must it wait for the reading to be within 0.1%?

step-response.L1: States that the step response is the output for a unit step input.
step-response.L2: Computes the step response of a first-order circuit or system from its τ and its gain for a constant input.
step-response.L3: Explains the step response as the running integral of the impulse response, says where it settles from the DC gain, and reads τ from where the starting tangent meets the final value.
step-response.L4: Uses linearity to build the response to a pulse or a square wave from shifted step responses, and knows when the settled value is undefined (an integrator, an unstable system).
missteps: takes the settled value as the input's size instead of the input times the DC gain
reads τ as the time to reach the final value
adds the responses to two steps without shifting the second in time

seeds.predict: A system with DC gain 0.5 and τ = 2 ms gets a 4 V step: where is the output after 2 ms and after 10 ms?
seeds.explain: Why the step response is the running integral of the impulse response.
seeds.limit: A pulse made shorter and shorter than τ, with its area kept fixed: what does the response approach?
seeds.transfer: A pulse of width 3τ into a first-order system: write its response as the difference of two step responses.
